title: 2 Peter

stories.title: 📜 2 Peter 1
summaryBullets: Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ have received a faith as precious as ours: (1:1).
Grace and peace be multiplied to you through the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord. (1:2).
His divine power has given us everything we need for life and godliness through the knowledge of Him who called us by His own glory and excellence. (1:3).

Through these He has given us His precious and magnificent promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, now that you have escaped the corruption in the world caused by evil desires. (1:4).
For this very reason, make every effort to add to your faith virtue; and to virtue, knowledge; (1:5).
and to knowledge, self-control; and to self-control, perseverance; and to perseverance, godliness; (1:6).
and to godliness, brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness, love. (1:7).
For if you possess these qualities and continue to grow in them, they will keep you from being ineffective and unproductive in your knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. (1:8).
But whoever lacks these traits is nearsighted to the point of blindness, having forgotten that he has been cleansed from his past sins. (1:9).
Therefore, brothers, strive to make your calling and election sure. For if you practice these things you will never stumble, (1:10).
and you will receive a lavish reception into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. (1:11).
Therefore I will always remind you of these things, even though you know them and are established in the truth you now have. (1:12).
I think it is right to refresh your memory as long as I live in the tent of my body, (1:13).
because I know that this tent will soon be laid aside, as our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me. (1:14).
And I will make every effort to ensure that after my departure, you will be able to recall these things at all times. (1:15).
For we did not follow cleverly devised fables when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of His majesty. (1:16).
For He received honor and glory from God the Father when the voice came to Him from the Majestic Glory, saying, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” (1:17).
And we ourselves heard this voice from heaven when we were with Him on the holy mountain. (1:18).

We also have the word of the prophets as confirmed beyond doubt. And you will do well to pay attention to it, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts. (1:19).
Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation. (1:20).
For no such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. (1:21).
crossRefs: John 15:5: Abiding in Christ bears fruit.
Philippians 2:12-13: Work out salvation, God works in you.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גְּבוּרָה אֱלֹהִית (gəḇūrāh ʾĕlōhît, sense), Greek: θείας δυνάμεως (theías dynámeōs, NT), Aramaic: חֵילוּ דֵאלָהָא (ḥēylū d-ʾAlāhā)
translationNotes.note: Refers to God’s inherent strength and authority that grants all things for life and godliness.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קְרִיאָה וּבְחִירָה (qərîʾāh ū-ḇeḥîrāh, sense), Greek: κλῆσιν καὶ ἐκλογήν (klêsin kai eklogḗn, NT), Aramaic: קריא ותבחר (qeryā w-teḇḥār)
translationNotes.note: Terms for God’s summons to faith and his choosing of his people; emphasize security in continuing in faith and virtue.

translationNotes.term: The tent of my body, and my departure
translationNotes.note: A skenoma is a tent, the kind you strike and carry, which is how Peter describes the body he is about to put down. The word he uses for his death in 1:15 is exodos, the same word as the book of Exodus, and it occurs only three times in the New Testament. One of the other two is Luke 9:31, where Moses and Elijah stand with Jesus on the mountain and speak of the exodos He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. Peter is writing about that mountain five verses later.

Peter is talking about one specific day: the transfiguration, recorded in Matthew 17:1-8, Mark 9:2-8, and Luke 9:28-36. Jesus took Peter, James, and John up a high mountain, which none of the accounts names, and His appearance changed while Moses and Elijah spoke with Him. The words Peter quotes in 1:17 are the words of the voice from the cloud, and they match Matthew 17:5. He is answering a charge of storytelling by saying he was standing there.

stories.keyTakeaway: Peter urges believers to add virtue, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly kindness, and love to their faith, making their calling and election sure; knowing his death is near, he testifies as an eyewitness of Jesus’ majesty and the voice from heaven on the holy mountain, and affirms that no prophecy of Scripture came by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.

stories.title: 🕊️ 2 Peter 2
summaryBullets: Now there were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you. They will secretly introduce destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them — bringing swift destruction on themselves. (2:1).
Many will follow in their depravity, and because of them the way of truth will be defamed. (2:2).
In their greed, these false teachers will exploit you with deceptive words. The longstanding verdict against them remains in force, and their destruction does not sleep. (2:3).
For if God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them deep into hell, placing them in chains of darkness to be held for judgment; (2:4).
if He did not spare the ancient world when He brought the flood on its ungodly people, but preserved Noah, a preacher of righteousness, among the eight; (2:5).
if He condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to destruction, reducing them to ashes as an example of what is coming on the ungodly; (2:6).
and if He rescued Lot, a righteous man distressed by the depraved conduct of the lawless (2:7).
(for that righteous man, living among them day after day, was tormented in his righteous soul by the lawless deeds he saw and heard )— (2:8).
if all this is so, then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to hold the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment. (2:9).
Such punishment is specially reserved for those who indulge the corrupt desires of the flesh and despise authority. Bold and self-willed, they are unafraid to slander glorious beings. (2:10).
Yet not even angels, though greater in strength and power, dare to bring such slanderous charges against them before the Lord. (2:11).

These men are like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be captured and destroyed. They blaspheme in matters they do not understand, and like such creatures, they too will be destroyed. (2:12).

The harm they will suffer is the wages of their wickedness. They consider it a pleasure to carouse in broad daylight. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deception as they feast with you. (2:13).
Their eyes are full of adultery; their desire for sin is never satisfied; they seduce the unstable. They are accursed children with hearts trained in greed. (2:14).
They have left the straight way and wandered off to follow the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness. (2:15).
But he was rebuked for his transgression by a donkey, otherwise without speech, that spoke with a man’s voice and restrained the prophet’s madness. (2:16).
These men are springs without water and mists driven by a storm. Blackest darkness is reserved for them. (2:17).
With lofty but empty words, they appeal to the sensual passions of the flesh and entice those who are just escaping from others who live in error. (2:18).
They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity. For a man is a slave to whatever has mastered him. (2:19).

If indeed they have escaped the corruption of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, only to be entangled and overcome by it again, their final condition is worse than it was at first. (2:20).
It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than to have known it and then to turn away from the holy commandment passed on to them. (2:21).
Of them the proverbs are true: “A dog returns to its vomit,” and, “A sow that is washed goes back to her wallowing in the mud.” (2:22).
crossRefs: Jude 1:4: Certain people pervert grace and deny Jesus.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִינִים (mînîm, sects/heresies, sense), Greek: αἱρέσεις ἀπωλείας (haíreseis apōleías, NT), Aramaic: מינותא (mînūtā)
translationNotes.note: Refers to divisive, destructive teachings that deviate from truth, leading to ruin.

In 2 Peter 2:4, the place of imprisonment for rebellious angels. The word is borrowed from Greek mythology, where Tartarus was the deepest abyss below Hades. Used only once in the New Testament; the context is the chaining of the Genesis 6 'sons of God' for final judgment.

A prophet from beyond the Euphrates whom Balak king of Moab hired to curse Israel (Numbers 22-24). His donkey saw the angel in the road first and spoke to him. He could not curse Israel, so Numbers 31:16 records that he advised the plan that pulled Israel into Baal-peor instead, and he was killed in the war with Midian (Numbers 31:8). Revelation 2:14 names the same tactic. In 1967 a plaster inscription written in ink was found at Deir Alla in the Jordan Valley, dating to roughly 800 BC, opening with the words of Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods.

This chapter and the letter of Jude cover the same ground in the same order, often in the same images. The angels who sinned (2:4 and Jude 1:6), Sodom and Gomorrah (2:6 and Jude 1:7), slandering glorious ones where even angels will not (2:10-11 and Jude 1:8-9), men acting like irrational animals (2:12 and Jude 1:10), the way of Balaam (2:15 and Jude 1:11), blots at the shared meals (2:13 and Jude 1:12), waterless springs and driven clouds (2:17 and Jude 1:12), and blackest darkness reserved (2:17 and Jude 1:13). Reading them side by side is how the overlap is meant to be seen.

stories.keyTakeaway: Peter warns of false teachers, likening them to past examples of judgment, exposing their greed, sensuality, and inevitable destruction.

stories.title: 📜 2 Peter 3
summaryBullets: Beloved, this is now my second letter to you. Both of them are reminders to stir you to wholesome thinking (3:1).
by recalling what was foretold by the holy prophets and commanded by our Lord and Savior through your apostles. (3:2).
Most importantly, you must understand that in the last days scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires. (3:3).
“Where is the promise of His coming?” they will ask. “Ever since our fathers fell asleep, everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation.” (3:4).
But they deliberately overlook the fact that long ago by God’s word the heavens existed and the earth was formed out of water and by water, (3:5).
through which the world of that time perished in the flood. (3:6).
And by that same word, the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire, being kept for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men. (3:7).
Beloved, do not let this one thing escape your notice: With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day. (3:8).
The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance. (3:9).
But the Day of the Lord will come like a thief. The heavens will disappear with a roar, the elements will be destroyed by fire, and the earth and its works will be laid bare. (3:10).
Since everything will be destroyed in this way, what kind of people ought you to be? You ought to conduct yourselves in holiness and godliness (3:11).
as you anticipate and hasten the coming of the day of God, when the heavens will be destroyed by fire and the elements will melt in the heat. (3:12).
But in keeping with God’s promise, we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells. (3:13).
Therefore, beloved, as you anticipate these things, make every effort to be found at peace— spotless and blameless in His sight. (3:14).
Consider also that our Lord’s patience brings salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote you with the wisdom God gave him. (3:15).

He writes this way in all his letters, speaking in them about such matters. Some parts of his letters are hard to understand, which ignorant and unstable people distort, as they do the rest of the Scriptures, to their own destruction. (3:16).
Therefore, beloved, since you already know these things, be on your guard so that you will not be carried away by the error of the lawless and fall from your secure standing. (3:17).
But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To Him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen. (3:18).
crossRefs: Psalm 90:4: A thousand years in God’s sight like yesterday.
1 Thessalonians 5:2: Day of the Lord comes like a thief.
Isaiah 65:17: Promise of new heavens and new earth.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יוֹם יְהוָה (yôm YHWH), Greek: ἡμέρα κυρίου (hēméra kyríou, NT), Aramaic: יומא דמריא (yōmā d-Maryā)
translationNotes.note: Prophetic term for God’s climactic day of judgment and salvation, used throughout the prophets and NT.

translationNotes.term: A thousand years as a day
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶלֶף שָׁנִים כְּיוֹם אֶחָד (ʾélep šānîm kəyôm ʾeḥād), Greek: χίλια ἔτη ὡς ἡμέρα μία (chília étē hōs hēméra mía, NT), Aramaic: אלף שנין כיום חד (ʾelep šnīn k-yōm ḥad)
translationNotes.note: Figure expressing God’s different relation to time; not bound to human scale of days and years.

Stoicheia are the things in a row that something is built from: the letters of the alphabet, the first steps of a subject, the basic parts of anything. Hebrews 5:12 uses it for the elementary teachings a beginner starts with. In Greek natural philosophy it named the four elements, earth, water, air, and fire, held to be what all matter was made of. English 'elements' can sound vague; the Greek means the constituent stuff itself.

Graphe means a writing, and in the New Testament it is the fixed technical term for the Scriptures, used that way about fifty times, as in 'All Scripture is God-breathed' (2 Timothy 3:16). Peter says here that people twist Paul's letters as they do the rest of the graphai. He is putting Paul's letters in the same category, and he calls him 'our beloved brother Paul' in the previous verse.

stories.keyTakeaway: Peter warns of scoffers, affirms the Lord’s patience, and describes the coming day of judgment and promise of new creation.

intro:
2 Peter was written by the apostle Peter (2 Peter 1:1: "Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours by the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ"). The letter was composed in Rome around AD 65-67, shortly before Peter's martyrdom by crucifixion under Nero. Peter writes with the awareness that his death is imminent: "I know that the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me" (2 Peter 1:14), a direct reference to Jesus' prediction of Peter's death recorded in John 21:18-19. The letter is addressed to the same audience as 1 Peter (the Christians of Asia Minor in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia), as Peter himself states: "This is now the second letter that I am writing to you, beloved. In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder" (2 Peter 3:1). For the full biographical sketch of Peter (originally Simon son of Jonah, fisherman from Bethsaida, married, brother of Andrew, member of the inner three with James and John, renamed Cephas/Peter by Jesus, preacher of the Pentecost sermon, opener of the gospel to the Gentiles through Cornelius's conversion, pillar of the Jerusalem church, traveling apostle), and for the primary-source documentation of his crucifixion in Rome under Nero (Clement of Rome, 1 Clement, chapter 5, Tertullian Prescription against Heretics 36, Origen preserved by Eusebius Ecclesiastical History 3.1.2, Jerome on the inverted crucifixion) and his traditional burial site at the Vatican Hill, see the introduction to 1 Peter. The letter's opening at 2 Peter 1:1 contains another of the New Testament's clearest affirmations of Christ's full deity: the Greek phrase "our God and Savior Jesus Christ" (tou theou hēmōn kai sōtēros Iēsou Christou) applies both titles, "God" and "Savior," to Jesus under the Granville Sharp rule, since the two singular nouns are joined by kai and only the first carries the article.

The historical setting is the closing years of Peter's life under Nero's persecution and the rising tide of false teaching in the Asian churches. The Roman emperor was Nero (AD 54-68), now firmly committed to the persecution of Christians that had begun after the great fire of Rome in AD 64. Peter's first letter had warned the churches of suffering from outside; this second letter warns them of corruption from within. False teachers had infiltrated the churches with a teaching that (1) denied the Lord's return and final judgment by mocking the apparent delay (2 Peter 3:3-4: "Scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires. They will say, 'Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation'"); (2) presumed upon grace as license for moral corruption (2 Peter 2:13-19); and (3) promised "freedom" while themselves being "slaves of corruption" (2 Peter 2:19). Peter denounces these teachers in chapter 2 with a sustained piling-up of Old Testament examples of judgment (the rebellious angels who left their proper dwelling, the world of the flood, Sodom and Gomorrah, and the example of Balaam's beast that rebuked the prophet's madness) - a chapter that closely parallels the letter of Jude in both language and content. Whether Peter quoted Jude or Jude quoted Peter or both drew on a common source is debated; what is clear is that the apostolic generation was concerned about the same false teachers in the same regions at the same time.

2 Peter is the sixty-first book of the Christian Bible, the twenty-second book of the New Testament, and the third of the seven General Epistles. The letter has three chapters. The earliest surviving manuscript is Papyrus 72 (P72, the Bodmer Papyrus, c. AD 250-300), the same codex that preserves 1 Peter and Jude; other early witnesses include Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (both 4th century AD). Several of 2 Peter's passages have become foundational to Christian doctrine: 2 Peter 1:16-18 records Peter's firsthand eyewitness testimony to the Transfiguration of Jesus on the holy mountain ("we were eyewitnesses of his majesty... we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain"), one of the New Testament's most explicit appeals to apostolic eyewitness as evidential foundation for the Christian message; 2 Peter 1:20-21 is the New Testament's clearest statement of the inspiration of Scripture as a divine-human cooperation ("knowing this first of all, that no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation. For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit"); 2 Peter 3:8 ("with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day"); 2 Peter 3:9 (God "is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance"); 2 Peter 3:10-13 (the Day of the Lord coming like a thief, with the heavens passing away and a new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells); and remarkably, 2 Peter 3:15-16, in which Peter explicitly classifies Paul's letters as "Scriptures," providing internal first-century New Testament recognition of the apostolic writings as inspired Scripture ("our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him, as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. There are some things in them that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures").
